In this vignette we will go through the process of identifying cell-wise epigenetic potential genes using single cell dataset. We start with two Single-cell datasets i.e. single cell atac-seq and single cell rna-seq. Both these datasets needs to be processed to get cell types. In case the cell-type annotation is not done/difficult for scATAC-seq, cell type labels can be transferred from scRNA-seq. There are multiple ways to do label transfer, we show one way of doing it using scglue pipeline in a separate jupyter notebook. 

```{r message = FALSE}
library(Seurat)
library(limma)
library(epiPot)
```


# Load data

In this vignette we assume that the user has single-cell datasets with cell-type annotations for both scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq. Another assumption here is that both datasets have some if not all cell types matching each other. (Note: make sure you dont have situation like cell types in scRNAseq has T-cell and scATAC-seq has T_cell or t_cell.)

```{r}
# TODO this data will not be provided with the package,
# but has to be downloaded, e.g., from Zenodo
# maybe usethis::use_course() ?
rna_data <- readRDS('/home/wolfgang/Plus/Projects/epipot_data/GSE161382_rna.rds')
atac_data <- readRDS('/home/wolfgang/Plus/Projects/epipot_data/GSE161381_atac.rds')
```


# Main workflow

The main workhorse of the package is the `epigenetic_potential()` function, which requires the following data:

1. A pair of count matrices from scATAC-seq and scRNA-seq in sparse format.
2. A pair of vectors with cell type annotations for those matrices.
3. A pair of vectors giving the samples contained in those matrices.

The function will then perform all preprocessing and analysis steps:

```{r, eval=FALSE}
# not run
res <- epigenetic_potential(
  rna_counts = rna_data@assays$RNA@counts,
  rna_cell_types = rna_data@meta.data$cells_short,
  rna_samples = rna_data@meta.data$orig.ident,
  atac_counts = atac_data@assays$peaks@counts,
  atac_cell_types = atac_data@meta.data$cell_type,
  atac_samples = atac_data@meta.data$orig.ident
)
```

Alternatively, if you want to fully control the individual steps of this function, you can implement the analysis workflow by using other functions provided by the package, which we will do below.

Create aggregate matrix from count matrix.

```{r}
rna_mat_agg <- aggregate_count_matrix(
  counts = rna_data@assays$RNA@counts, 
  cell_types = rna_data@meta.data$cells_short,
  samples = rna_data@meta.data$orig.ident
)
atac_mat_agg <- aggregate_count_matrix(
  counts = atac_data@assays$peaks@counts, 
  cell_types = atac_data@meta.data$cell_type,
  samples = atac_data@meta.data$orig.ident
)
```

Scale the rows of aggregate matrices so that they contains Z-scores.

```{r}
rna_mat_z <- scale_rows(rna_mat_agg)
atac_mat_z <- scale_rows(atac_mat_agg)
```

Annotate peaks in ATAC-seq data with genes.

```{r warning=FALSE,message=FALSE}
atac_mat_z_anno <- annotate_atac_peaks(atac_mat_z)
```

Create a merged matrix containing both scRNA-seq and scATAC-seq data.

```{r}
merged_mat <- merge_count_matrices(rna_mat_z, atac_mat_z_anno)
```

Create a model frame for the model matrix.

```{r}
sample_metadata <- create_model_frame(merged_mat)
```

Create the model matrix.

```{r}
model <- model.matrix(
  ~ 0 + cell / tech,
  data = sample_metadata 
)
```

Run limma.

```{r warning = FALSE}
fit <-
  merged_mat |>
  lmFit(model) |> 
  eBayes()
```

Parse limma results.

```{r}
res <- parse_limma_results(fit)
# saveRDS(atac_mat_agg, "../data/epipot_atac_mat_agg.rds")
# saveRDS(merged_mat, "../data/epipot_merged.rds")
# saveRDS(res, "../data/epipot_res.rds")
```

After these steps, `res`  will contain the same data as if we had run the `epigenetic_potential()` function.
